<skill_content name="customize-opencode">
# Skill: customize-opencode

<!--
  Built-in skill. Name and description are registered in code at
  packages/core/src/plugin/skill.ts
  and CUSTOMIZE_OPENCODE_SKILL_DESCRIPTION). The body below becomes the
  skill's content.
-->

# Customizing opencode

opencode validates its own config strictly and refuses to start when a field
is wrong. The shapes below cover the common surface area, but they are a
**summary, not the source of truth**.

## Full schema reference

The authoritative list of every config option — with field types, enums,
defaults, and descriptions — lives in the published JSON Schema:

**<https://opencode.ai/config.json>**

If a field is not documented in this skill, or you need to confirm an exact
shape before writing config, **fetch that URL and read the schema directly**
rather than guessing. opencode hard-fails on invalid config, so the cost of a
wrong shape is a broken startup.

Independently, every `opencode.json` should declare
`"$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json"` so the user's editor catches
mistakes as they type.

## Applying changes

Config is loaded once when opencode starts and is not hot-reloaded. After
saving changes to `opencode.json`, an agent file, a skill, a plugin, or any
other config-time file, **tell the user to quit and restart opencode** for
the changes to take effect. The running session will keep using the
already-loaded config until then.

## Where files live

| Scope                         | Path                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project config                | `./opencode.json`, `./opencode.jsonc`, or `.opencode/opencode.json` (opencode walks up from the cwd to the worktree root) |
| Global config                 | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (NOT `~/.opencode/`)                                                                   |
| Project agents                | `.opencode/agent/<name>.md` or `.opencode/agents/<name>.md`                                                               |
| Global agents                 | `~/.config/opencode/agent(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                   |
| Project commands              | `.opencode/command/<name>.md` or `.opencode/commands/<name>.md`                                                           |
| Global commands               | `~/.config/opencode/command(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                 |
| Project skills                | `.opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                                      |
| Global skills                 | `~/.config/opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                             |
| External skills (auto-loaded) | `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                    |

Configs from each scope are deep-merged. Project overrides global. Unknown
top-level keys in `opencode.json` are rejected with `ConfigInvalidError`.

## opencode.json

Every field is optional.

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "username": "string",
  "model": "provider/model-id",
  "small_model": "provider/model-id",
  "default_agent": "agent-name",
  "shell": "/bin/zsh",
  "logLevel": "DEBUG" | "INFO" | "WARN" | "ERROR",
  "share": "manual" | "auto" | "disabled",
  "autoupdate": true | false | "notify",
  "snapshot": true,
  "instructions": ["AGENTS.md", "docs/style.md"],

  "skills": {
    "paths": [".opencode/skills", "/abs/path/to/skills"],
    "urls": ["https://example.com/.well-known/skills/"]
  },

  "references": {
    "docs": {
      "path": "../docs",
      "description": "Use for product behavior and documentation conventions"
    },
    "sdk": {
      "repository": "owner/sdk",
      "branch": "main",
      "description": "Use for SDK implementation details",
      "hidden": true
    }
  },

  "agent": {
    "my-agent": {
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "description": "...",
      "permission": { "edit": "deny" }
    }
  },

  "command": {
    "deploy": { "description": "...", "template": "..." }
  },

  "provider": {
    "anthropic": { "options": { "apiKey": "..." } }
  },
  "disabled_providers": ["openai"],
  "enabled_providers": ["anthropic"],

  "mcp": {
    "playwright": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["npx", "-y", "@playwright/mcp"],
      "enabled": true,
      "env": {}
    },
    "remote-thing": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://...",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ..." }
    }
  },

  "plugin": [
    "opencode-gemini-auth",
    "opencode-foo@1.2.3",
    "./local-plugin.ts",
    ["opencode-bar", { "option": "value" }]
  ],

  "permission": {
    "edit": "deny",
    "bash": { "git *": "allow", "*": "ask" }
  },

  "formatter": false,
  "lsp": false,

  "experimental": {
    "primary_tools": ["edit"],
    "mcp_timeout": 30000
  },

  "tool_output": { "max_lines": 200, "max_bytes": 8192 },

  "compaction": { "auto": true, "tail_turns": 15 }
}
```

Shape notes worth being explicit about:

- `model` always carries a provider prefix: `"anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"`.
- `skills` is an object with `paths` and/or `urls`, not an array.
- `references` is an object keyed by alias. Each value is a local path, Git repository, or string shorthand.
- `agent` is an object keyed by agent name, not an array.
- `command` is an object keyed by command name, not an array.
- `plugin` is an array of strings or `[name, options]` tuples, not an object.
- `mcp[name].command` is an array of strings, never a single string. `type` is required.
- `permission` is either a string action or an object keyed by tool name.

## Skills

opencode's skill loader scans for `**/SKILL.md` inside skill directories. The
file is named `SKILL.md` exactly, and lives in its own folder named after the
skill:

```
.opencode/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md
```

Frontmatter:

```markdown
---
name: my-skill
description: One sentence covering what this skill does AND when to trigger it. Front-load the literal keywords or filenames the user is likely to say.
---

# My Skill

(skill body in markdown: instructions, examples, references)
```

- `name` is required, lowercase hyphen-separated, up to 64 chars, and matches the folder name.
- `description` is effectively required: skills without one are filtered out and never surfaced to the model. Cover both _what_ the skill does and _when_ to use it. Write in third person ("Use when...", not "I help with..."). Front-load concrete trigger keywords and filenames; gate with "Use ONLY when..." if the skill should stay quiet on adjacent topics.
- Optional: `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata` (string-string map).

Register skills from non-default locations via `skills.paths` (scanned
recursively for `**/SKILL.md`) and `skills.urls` (each URL serves a list of
skills).

## References

References make local directories and Git repositories outside the active
project available as supporting context. Configure them under `references`,
keyed by the alias used in `@` autocomplete:

```json
{
  "references": {
    "docs": {
      "path": "../product-docs",
      "description": "Use for product behavior and terminology"
    },
    "effect": {
      "repository": "Effect-TS/effect",
      "branch": "main",
      "description": "Use for Effect implementation details"
    }
  }
}
```

Local `path` values may be relative to the declaring config, absolute, or use
`~/`. Git `repository` values accept Git URLs, host/path references, and GitHub
`owner/repo` shorthand; `branch` is optional. Both forms support optional
`description` and `hidden` fields.

- Only references with a `description` are advertised to agents in system context.
- `hidden: true` removes a reference from TUI `@` autocomplete only. It remains available to agents and by direct path.
- Reference directories are automatically allowed through the external-directory boundary; normal read/edit/tool permissions still apply.
- String shorthand is supported: use `"docs": "../docs"` for local paths or `"effect": "Effect-TS/effect"` for Git repositories.

## Agents

Two ways to define an agent. Use the file form for anything non-trivial.

### Inline (in `opencode.json`)

```json
{
  "agent": {
    "my-reviewer": {
      "description": "Reviews PRs for style violations.",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
      "permission": { "edit": "deny", "bash": "ask" },
      "prompt": "You are a strict PR reviewer..."
    }
  }
}
```

### File

```
.opencode/agent/my-reviewer.md      OR     .opencode/agents/my-reviewer.md
```

```markdown
---
description: Reviews PRs for style violations.
mode: subagent
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
permission:
  edit: deny
  bash: ask
---

You are a strict PR reviewer. Focus on...
```

The file body becomes the agent's `prompt`. Do not also put `prompt:` in the
frontmatter.

`mode` is one of `"primary"`, `"subagent"`, `"all"`.

Allowed top-level frontmatter fields: `name, model, variant, description, mode,
hidden, color, steps, options, permission, disable, temperature, top_p`. Any
unknown field is silently routed into `options`.

To disable a built-in agent: `agent: { build: { disable: true } }`, or in a
file, `disable: true` in frontmatter.

`default_agent` must point to a non-hidden, primary-mode agent.

### Built-in agents

opencode ships with `build`, `plan`, `general`, `explore`. Hidden internal agents:
`compaction`, `title`, `summary`. To override a built-in's fields, define the
same key in `agent: { <name>: { ... } }`.

## Commands

opencode's command loader scans for `**/*.md` inside command directories. The
file is named after the command, and lives directly inside the `command` folder:

```
.opencode/command/deploy.md
```

Frontmatter:

```markdown
---
description: One sentence describing what the command does.
agent: build
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
---

(command body in markdown: the prompt opencode runs, with $ARGUMENTS for the user's input)
```

- `template` is the command body — everything below the frontmatter — and is required: it is the prompt opencode runs when the command is invoked. Do not also put a `template:` key in the frontmatter.
- `$ARGUMENTS` is replaced with everything the user typed after the command; `$1`, `$2`, … pull individual positional arguments.
- Optional: `description`, `agent`, `model`, `variant`, `subtask`.

## Plugins

`plugin:` is an array. Each entry is one of:

```json
"plugin": [
  "opencode-gemini-auth",            // npm spec, latest
  "opencode-foo@1.2.3",              // npm spec, pinned
  "./local-plugin.ts",               // file path, relative to the declaring config
  "file:///abs/path/plugin.js",      // file URL
  ["opencode-bar", { "key": "val" }] // tuple form with options
]
```

Auto-discovered plugins (no config entry needed): any `*.ts` or `*.js` file in
`.opencode/plugin/` or `.opencode/plugins/`.

A plugin module exports `default` (or any named export) of type
`Plugin = (input: PluginInput, options?) => Promise<Hooks>`. The export is a
function, not a plain object literal, and the function returns an object
(return `{}` if there is nothing to register).

```ts
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"

export default (async ({ client, project, directory, $ }) => {
  return {
    config: (cfg) => {
      // cfg is the live merged config; mutate fields here.
    },
    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {
      // mutate output.args before the tool runs
    },
  }
}) satisfies Plugin
```

Hook surface (mutate `output` in place; return `void`):

- `event(input)`: every bus event
- `config(cfg)`: once on init with the merged config
- `chat.message`, `chat.params`, `chat.headers`
- `tool.execute.before`, `tool.execute.after`
- `tool.definition`
- `command.execute.before`
- `shell.env`
- `permission.ask`
- `experimental.chat.messages.transform`, `experimental.chat.system.transform`,
  `experimental.session.compacting`, `experimental.compaction.autocontinue`,
  `experimental.text.complete`

Special object-shaped (not callbacks): `tool: { my_tool: { ... } }`,
`auth: { ... }`, `provider: { ... }`.

## MCP servers

`mcp:` is an object keyed by server name. Each server is discriminated by
`type`:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "playwright": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["npx", "-y", "@playwright/mcp"],
      "enabled": true,
      "env": { "BROWSER": "chromium" }
    },
    "github": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://...",
      "enabled": true,
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:GITHUB_TOKEN}" }
    },
    "old-server": { "enabled": false }
  }
}
```

`command` is an array of strings. `type` is required. Use `enabled: false` to
disable a server inherited from a parent config. String values such as header
tokens support `{env:VAR}` interpolation (and `{file:path}`); the shell-style
`${VAR}` is not substituted.

## Permissions

```json
"permission": {
  "edit": "deny",
  "bash": { "git *": "allow", "rm *": "deny", "*": "ask" },
  "external_directory": { "~/secrets/**": "deny", "*": "allow" }
}
```

Actions: `"allow"`, `"ask"`, `"deny"`.

Per-tool value forms: `"allow"` shorthand (treated as `{"*": "allow"}`), or an
object `{ pattern: action }`. Within an object, **insertion order matters**.
opencode evaluates the LAST matching rule, so put broad rules first and narrow
rules last.

`permission: "allow"` (a string at the top level) is shorthand for "allow
everything" and is rarely what the user wants.

Known permission keys: `read, edit, glob, grep, list, bash, task,
external_directory, todowrite, question, webfetch, websearch, lsp, doom_loop,
skill`. Some of these (`todowrite,
question, webfetch, websearch, doom_loop`) only accept a flat
action, not a per-pattern object.

`external_directory` patterns are filesystem paths (use `~/`, absolute paths,
or globs like `~/projects/**`).

Per-agent `permission:` overrides top-level `permission:`. Plan Mode lives on
the `plan` agent's permission ruleset (`edit: deny *`).

## Escape hatches

When a user's config is broken and opencode won't start, these env vars help:

- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG=1`: skip the project's local `opencode.json`
  and start from globals only. Run from the project directory, opencode loads,
  the user edits the broken file, then they restart without the flag.
- `OPENCODE_CONFIG=/path/to/file.json`: load an additional explicit config.
- `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT='{"$schema":"https://opencode.ai/config.json"}'`:
  inject inline JSON as a final local-scope merge.
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS=1`: skip default plugins.
- `OPENCODE_PURE=1`: skip external plugins entirely.
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_EXTERNAL_SKILLS=1`,
  `OPENCODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_CODE_SKILLS=1`: skip the external skill scans under
  `~/.claude/` and `~/.agents/`.

## When proposing edits

- Validate against the schema before writing. If you are unsure of a field's
  exact shape, or the field is not covered in this skill, fetch
  `https://opencode.ai/config.json` and read the schema rather than guessing.
- Preserve `$schema` and any existing fields the user did not ask to change.
- For agent, command, skill, and plugin definitions, prefer creating new files
  in the correct location over inlining everything in `opencode.json`.
- If the user's existing config is malformed, point them at the env-var escape
  hatches above so they can edit from inside opencode without breaking their
  session.
- After saving any config change, remind the user to quit and restart opencode
  — running sessions keep using the already-loaded config.

# WordPress.com MCP tools reference

Copy page

This document provides a comprehensive mapping of MCP tools available for WordPress.com developers. This is a living document and will be updated as new tools are added or existing ones are modified.

For exact input and output schemas, call the tool itself — every STRAP facade exposes `action: list` (operation catalog) and `action: describe` (full JSON Schema per operation). Schemas evolve, so always treat the live `describe` response as the source of truth.

## How WordPress.com MCP tools are organized

The WordPress.com MCP server exposes two kinds of tools:

-   **STRAP facade tools** — A single MCP tool that wraps a family of related operations behind one entry point. Facades use a uniform action-based interface (`action: list | describe | execute`) so AI agents discover what’s available, fetch parameter schemas, and execute operations through one tool. This keeps the tool catalog small and predictable.
-   **Standalone tools** — Single-purpose tools that take parameters directly. Used for operations that don’t fit a larger family (e.g. listing the user’s sites, generating a checkout URL).

⚠️ **Safety protocol:** All write, update, and delete operations require user confirmation. The agent must (1) describe exactly what it plans to do, (2) ask the user for explicit confirmation, and (3) include the user’s confirmation as `user_confirmed: true` in the execute `params`. Write operations are never auto-executed. Permanent deletions (taxonomy terms) additionally require `confirm_permanent_delete: true`.

## Action-based interface (STRAP facades)

Every STRAP facade tool accepts the same three top-level inputs:

-   `action` (enum: `list` / `describe` / `execute`): What the agent wants to do.
-   `list` — Discover available operations on this tool. Returns operation names, short descriptions, and disabled-operation reasons.
-   `describe` — Get the full JSON Schema (parameters, types, required fields) for one operation.
-   `execute` — Run an operation.
-   `operation`: The operation name in `resource.action` form (e.g., `posts.create`, `theme.presets`).
-   `params`: Operation-specific parameters. Write operations must include `user_confirmed: true`.

Most facades also require `wpcom_site` (a site ID or URL). The `wpcom-mcp-account` facade is the exception — it operates on the authenticated user.

All operations support an optional `include_fields` parameter to limit which fields are returned. Use it to keep responses context-efficient.

---

## STRAP facade tools

### Content Authoring ( `wpcom-mcp-content-authoring` )

Create, read, update, and delete content on a WordPress.com site — posts, pages, comments, media, categories, tags, block patterns, and content search.

💡 **Recommended sequence:** Call `wpcom-mcp-site-editor-context` first (`theme.active`, `theme.presets`) so content uses theme-aligned preset slugs (e.g. `"primary"`, `"large"`) instead of hard-coded colors and sizes.

#### Available operations

Operation

Description

`posts.list`

List posts with optional filters (status, author, search, taxonomy, date range, ordering, pagination).

`posts.get`

Get a single post by ID or slug. Falls back to searching pages if a slug doesn’t match a post.

`posts.create`

Create a new post — creates as **draft** by default. Write.

`posts.update`

Update an existing post. Only provided fields change. If status is `publish`, changes go **live immediately**. Write.

`posts.delete`

Move a post to trash. Restorable from WordPress admin within 30 days. Write.

`pages.list`

List pages with optional filters (parent, status, search, ordering, pagination).

`pages.get`

Get a single page by ID or slug.

`pages.create`

Create a new page — creates as **draft** by default. Supports hierarchical structures and page templates. Write.

`pages.update`

Update an existing page. Only provided fields change. If status is `publish`, changes go live immediately. Write.

`pages.delete`

Move a page to trash. Restorable from WordPress admin within 30 days. Write.

`comments.list`

List comments with optional filters (status, post, author, search, date range, pagination).

`comments.get`

Get a single comment by ID.

`comments.create`

Create a comment on a post. Comments from authenticated users auto-populate author fields. Write.

`comments.update`

Update an existing comment. If status is `approved`, changes are visible immediately. Write.

`comments.delete`

Move a comment to trash. Write.

`media.list`

List media items with optional filters (mime type, post, author, search, date range, pagination).

`media.get`

Get a single media item by ID.

`media.create`

Upload a new media item (image, video, audio, document). Write.

`media.update`

Update media item metadata (not the file). Changes to `alt_text` and `caption` update **immediately** wherever the media is used. Write.

`media.delete`

Move a media item to trash. **May break content** that references it. Write.

`categories.list`

List categories with optional filters.

`categories.get`

Get a single category by ID.

`categories.create`

Create a new category. Supports hierarchical parent-child relationships. Write.

`categories.update`

Update an existing category. Changing the slug affects archive URLs **immediately** and may break links. Write.

`categories.delete`

**Permanently** delete a category — taxonomy terms have no trash. Assigned posts move to Uncategorized; child categories become top-level. Requires `confirm_permanent_delete: true`.

`tags.list`

List tags with optional filters. Tag search is case-insensitive.

`tags.get`

Get a single tag by ID.

`tags.create`

Create a new tag. Write.

`tags.update`

Update an existing tag. Changing the slug affects archive URLs immediately. Write.

`tags.delete`

**Permanently** delete a tag — removed from all associated posts. Requires `confirm_permanent_delete: true`.

`patterns.list`

List block patterns available on the site (theme, core, pattern directory).

`patterns.get`

Get a single block pattern by name, including its block markup.

`synced-patterns.list`

List the site’s synced (reusable) patterns.

`synced-patterns.get`

Get a single synced pattern by ID, including its block markup.

`content-search`

Free-text search across the site’s content (posts, pages, other post types).

⚠️ **Destructive operations** (`posts.delete`, `pages.delete`, `comments.delete`, `media.delete`, `categories.delete`, `tags.delete`) require the agent to fetch and present the item being deleted (title, author, count of affected posts) before requesting confirmation.

💡 **Tip:** When creating pages, use `patterns.list` → `patterns.get` to fetch block patterns and compose full pages from multiple patterns. After every create or update, check the response’s `_content_warnings` field — WordPress may strip blocks or HTML during save.

---

### Site Editor Context ( `wpcom-mcp-site-editor-context` )

Query site design context — theme presets, applied styles, and registered block types. **Read-only** companion to Content Authoring. Use it **before** creating or updating content so the markup uses theme-aligned tokens rather than hard-coded values.

This facade uses `action: list | describe | get` (not `execute`, since it never writes).

💡 **Recommended sequence:** `theme.active` → `theme.presets` → (optionally) `blocks.allowed` → then create content via `wpcom-mcp-content-authoring`.

#### Available operations

Operation

Description

`theme.active`

Get the active theme’s stylesheet slug and name. Use the `stylesheet` value when fetching `theme.presets` or `theme.styles`.

`theme.presets`

Get the site’s design tokens — color palette, font sizes, font families, gradients, spacing scale. Auto-resolves stylesheet from the active theme if omitted.

`theme.styles`

Get the site’s applied styles from `theme.json` — block-level overrides and element-level typography/colors. Complements `theme.presets`: presets are *what tokens exist*; styles are *how they’re applied*.

`blocks.allowed`

List block types registered on the site with name, title, description, category, and style variations. Apply a style variation as `is-style-{name}`.

💡 **Tip:** Reference preset slugs in block markup — e.g., `has-primary-color` or `has-large-font-size` — rather than inline styles with raw hex or pixel values, so content adapts when the site’s design tokens change.

⚠️ **Important:** A block being registered does not guarantee its markup survives the REST API save pipeline unchanged. After every create or update via `wpcom-mcp-content-authoring`, check the `_content_warnings` field. If markup was stripped, use simpler block alternatives or ask the user how to proceed.

---

### Account ( `wpcom-mcp-account` )

Manage the authenticated user’s WordPress.com account — profile, notifications, achievements, domains, connections, security, and currency. Operates on the calling user; no `wpcom_site` parameter required.

#### Available operations

Operation

Description

`profile.get`

Basic profile (username, email, display name, avatar, locale, timezone), optionally with preferences, stats, account info, social/activity data.

`profile.update`

Update profile fields (display name, bio, locale, etc.). Write.

`notifications.get`

Notification preferences across email, push, timeline, and other channels. Includes device list and delivery test.

`notifications.update`

Update notification settings. Write.

`inbox.get`

The user’s notification inbox (messages, alerts, mentions, likes, follows). Filter by type, unread, time range.

`achievements.get`

Earned badges, feats, gamification progress, and trophy case.

`domains.list`

List the authenticated user’s domains across all sites.

`domains.get`

Domain details: management capabilities, DNS configuration, DNSSEC, SSL status, maintenance state.

`domains.dns_records`

DNS records (A, AAAA, ALIAS, CAA, CNAME, MX, NS, SRV, TXT) for a single domain.

`domains.set_primary`

Set a custom domain as the primary domain for a site. Write.

`connections.get`

Social and third-party service connections (list, get details, test health).

`security.get`

Security status: 2FA, application passwords, active sessions, login history, account age.

`currency.preview`

Preview the impact of changing account currency (does not commit).

`currency.change`

Change account currency. Write.

---

### Site ( `wpcom-mcp-site` )

Manage a WordPress.com site — settings, statistics, plugins, activity log, themes, and Jetpack module configuration. Requires `wpcom_site` (site ID or URL).

#### Available operations

Operation

Description

`settings.get`

General, writing, reading, discussion, media, permalink, and privacy settings.

`settings.update`

Update site settings. Write.

`statistics.get`

Site totals — published posts, pages, subscribers — plus optional views, visitors, posts published, and pages published for a date range. Does NOT include top-posts, referrers, geo, or per-URL breakdowns.

`plugin.list`

Installed plugins with status, version, update availability, and permissions.

`activity.get`

Activity log entries (posts, comments, plugin updates, backups, user actions). Reverse-chronological. Defaults to the last 6 months. Filter by `activity_group` and `activity_action`.

`theme.list`

Installed themes on the site.

`theme.set`

Switch the active theme. Write.

`monitor.status` / `monitor.activate` / `monitor.deactivate`

Jetpack Monitor uptime checks. Activate/deactivate are writes.

`newsletter.status` / `newsletter.get_settings`

Jetpack Newsletter status and settings.

`account-protection.status` / `account-protection.activate` / `account-protection.deactivate`

Jetpack Account Protection. Activate/deactivate are writes.

`manage-site.status` / `manage-site.launch` / `manage-site.set-visibility`

Site lifecycle — coming-soon status, launch, visibility. Writes.

💡 **Tip for `activity.get`:** combine `activity_group` (e.g. `["plugin"]`) and `activity_action` (e.g. `["activated", "deactivated"]`) to narrow investigations. Call without filters first to discover what’s available for a given site.

---

## Standalone tools

### List user sites ( `wpcom-user-sites` )

List the authenticated user’s accessible sites across WordPress.com and self-hosted Jetpack-connected sites. Use this to discover site IDs before calling site-scoped tools. Supports pagination, search, status and privacy filters, sorting, and optional site metrics.

---

### Search domain availability ( `wpcom-domain-purchase` )

Search for available domains and generate checkout links for registration on WordPress.com. Returns matching domains with prices and pre-built checkout URLs.

---

### Update DNS records ( `wpcom-domain-update-dns-records` )

Add or remove DNS records (A, AAAA, ALIAS, CAA, CNAME, MX, NS, SRV, TXT) for a single custom domain you manage.

⚠️ **Destructive operation.** Misconfigured DNS can break email and websites. Always fetch the current records (via `wpcom-mcp-account` → `domains.dns_records`) and describe the diff before requesting confirmation.

---

### Restore default DNS records ( `wpcom-domain-restore-default-dns-records` )

Restore the WordPress.com default A records (apex IPs) or the default `www` CNAME for a single custom domain. Gated by the “Update DNS records” setting.

---

### Update nameservers ( `wpcom-domain-update-nameservers` )

Set the nameservers for a single custom domain. Requires the caller to manage the site the domain is connected to. Accepts between 2 and 13 valid nameserver hostnames.

⚠️ Changing nameservers transfers DNS control away from WordPress.com. Email, websites, and other services may break if the new nameservers aren’t configured to serve the same records.

---

### Set external mail service ( `wpcom-domain-set-mail-service` )

Configure DNS records on a domain for an external mail service: Google Workspace, iCloud Mail, Office 365, or Zoho Mail.

⚠️ Overwrites the domain’s existing MX and related DNS records. Existing mail flow stops as soon as the new records propagate.

---

### Generate checkout URL ( `wpcom-checkout-url` )

Generate a pre-configured WordPress.com checkout URL for one or more products (new purchase) or for a subscription renewal. The URL takes the user to the WordPress.com checkout — payment happens in the browser, not via this tool.

---

### List WordPress.com plans ( `wpcom-plans-list` )

List WordPress.com plans with prices and per-tier feature lists. Read-only; useful for surfacing plan options before generating a checkout URL.

---

## Safety protocol summary

All write/delete operations enforce a mandatory confirmation flow. The agent must describe the action, get explicit user approval, and pass that approval as `user_confirmed: true` in the execute `params`.

`confirm_permanent_delete: true`

Permanent deletions (taxonomy terms like categories and tags) additionally require `confirm_permanent_delete: true` in `params`.

Accepted forms of `user_confirmed`: the boolean `true` (preferred), or one of the strings `"true"`, `"yes"`, `"on"`, `"1"`. Free-form approval phrases like `"yes do it"` are rejected — the agent must translate the user’s approval into one of these accepted forms.

OK, so the tools reference page is for the **WordPress.com MCP** (the cloud/hosted version), not the **Studio MCP** (local version). The Studio MCP seems to have different tools - it mentions "WP-CLI commands, screenshots" in the earlier docs.

However, the Studio MCP server is a separate thing from the WordPress.com MCP. The Studio MCP provides:
- WP-CLI command execution
- Screenshots
- Site management (create, start, stop)
- Reading instruction files and skills

Here's a summary of all fixes applied:

---

## MCP Config

**Created** `.opencode/mcp.json` with the Studio MCP server config. Restart opencode to pick it up.

## Issue 1 — Dia Text goes invisible after animation

**Files:** `theme.css` (line 288), `frontend.js` (line 90)

**Root cause:** CSS had `color: transparent` as a fallback on `.wp21-dia-text-content`. After animation, the JS cleared `color = ''` but the CSS rule kept it transparent.

**Fix:** Removed `color: transparent` from CSS. Now after the sweep, clearing the inline `style.color` makes the text inherit the parent's foreground color — visible in both light and dark mode.

## Issue 2 — Typewriter shows full text with blinking cursor, never types

**Files:** `wp21-animations.php` (line 135), `frontend.js` (lines 129, 152)

**Root cause:** The render callback output all words as initial HTML (`"Ideas become reality with 21st.dev"`). The JS started from `charIndex=0` after a 1-second delay, so the user saw the full text first, then a jump to empty, then typing. The 1s delay made it feel broken.

**Fix:** 
- Render callback: output empty initial text
- JS: `textEl.textContent = ''` immediately, then call `type()` with no delay — typing starts instantly, no flash

## Issue 3 — Text Glitch just fades on hover, no animation

**Files:** `theme.css` (lines 228-260), `wp21-animations.php` (line 176)

**Root cause:** Only had `transition: opacity 0.2s` — no actual glitch animation.

**Fix:** Added real glitch effect with:
- `data-text` attribute on the wrapper span (render callback)
- `::before` pseudo-element (red channel, top slice) with `clip-path`
- `::after` pseudo-element (cyan channel, bottom slice) with `clip-path`
- `@keyframes glitch-text-shake`, `glitch-slice-top`, `glitch-slice-bottom` — jitter and offset animations on hover (0.4s, 2 iterations)

## Issue 4 — Text Cycle blue color

**File:** `theme.css` (line 296)

**Root cause:** Unclear without seeing rendered output, but the `.wp21-cycle-text` span had no explicit color declaration, which could inherit unintended colors from parent context.

**Fix:** Added `color: inherit` to `.wp21-cycle-text` so it always matches the surrounding text.

The JS animation code is the same. The difference is how the HTML is rendered and how the editor UI works for configuring the animations.

**Comparison:**

| Aspect | Current (Gutenberg blocks) | Elementor |
|--------|---------------------------|-----------|
| Block/widget development | register_block_type + PHP render callback | Elementor widget class (PHP) |
| Editor UI | block.json attributes | widget controls (PHP) |

This is the fundamental challenge — converting any React site to pixel-perfect WordPress. Here's what I've learned from this project that would form the basis of a repeatable approach:

## The Core Problem

A React site has **three layers** that each need their own conversion:

| Layer | React | WordPress |
|---|---|---|
| **Layout** | JSX + Tailwind classes | HTML block markup / theme.json |
| **Styles** | Tailwind utility classes → CSS | theme.json presets + CSS variables |
| **Animations** | JS components + CSS transitions | Same JS + CSS, just different HTML structure |

## Proposed Architecture

### 1. Style Foundation — Match Every Token First

Before writing any blocks, create a `theme.json` that exactly mirrors the React site's Tailwind config:

- **Colors:** Map every `text-*`, `bg-*`, `border-*` color to `preset` tokens
- **Font sizes:** Exact rem values from Tailwind's scale
- **Spacing:** `gap-*`, `p-*`, `m-*` become the spacing scale
- **Breakpoints:** `sm/md/lg/xl` map to theme.json `viewportWidth`

Then generate a companion `theme.css` that:
- Defines `--tw-*` CSS variables matching the Tailwind config
- Adds any `@apply`-style compound utilities (`.section-label`, `.card-hover`)

**This eliminates guesswork** — every Tailwind class has a CSS variable equivalent.

### 2. Layout — Convert the Visual Tree

Two options depending on editing needs:

**Option A — Block Theme (current approach):**
- Manually map each section to core blocks (`cover`, `columns`, `group`, `heading`, `paragraph`)
- Use `theme.json` presets for colors and font sizes so they're editor-editable
- Wrap animations in `wp21/*` custom blocks
- **Pixel perfection:** Fine-tune inline styles for padding, margins, gap — WordPress block spacing controls are in `px`/`rem`

**Option B — Elementor (better for visual editing):**
- Create a custom Elementor widget for each unique section
- Use Elementor's `Controls_Manager` for layout, color, typography controls
- Register the animation JS globally
- **Pixel perfection:** Elementor's responsive mode + custom CSS per widget gives tighter control

### 3. Animations — The Easy Part

The JS animations are **framework-agnostic** — they query the DOM via `data-*` attributes and use `requestAnimationFrame` / CSS keyframes. Same code works in Gutenberg, Elementor, or raw HTML. The only difference is how the initial HTML is rendered (block/widget render callback vs shortcode).

### 4. The Pixel-Perfect Gap

No automated conversion will be pixel-perfect out of the box because:

- WordPress themes apply their own CSS (reset, typography, block styles)
- Core blocks have their own padding/margin internal structure
- `theme.json` spacing presets don't match every arbitrary Tailwind value

**The fix:** For each section, compare the React output with WordPress output visually (screenshot), then apply targeted CSS overrides. This is where the Studio MCP screenshot tool would help.

### 5. Recommended Workflow

1. **Extract** the Tailwind config from the React project → generate `theme.json`
2. **Identify** which sections have custom JS animations → those become custom blocks/widgets
3. **Build** the static sections with core blocks / Elementor
4. **Register** the animation JS as a global asset
5. **Verify** with screenshots at each breakpoint, tweak until pixel-perfect
6. **Repeat** for each new React project — the theme.json generator and animation plugin become reusable assets

## 5. DETAILED COMPONENT FILE ANALYSIS

### 5.1 `dia-text.tsx` (332 lines) — `DiaText` / `DiaTextReveal`

| Aspect | Details |
|---|---|
| **Animation library** | `motion/react` (`motion`, `animate`, `useInView`, `useMotionValue`, `useTransform`) |
| **Prop defaults** | `colors` = `["#c679c4", "#fa3d1d", "#ffb005", "#e1e1fe", "#0358f7"]`, `textColor` = `"#ffffff"`, `duration` = `2`, `delay` = `0`, `repeatDelay` = `0.5`, `triggerOnView` = `true`, `once` = `true`, `fixedWidth` = `false` |
| **CSS classes on outer span** | `align-bottom text-inherit leading-[100%]` + user `className` |
| **CSS classes on inner span** | `inline-block text-inherit leading-[100%]` |
| **CSS class for screen-reader** | `sr-only` |
| **Motion values** | `sweepPos` (SWEEP_START=-17 to SWEEP_END=117), `textOpacity`, `textBlur`, `textShift` |
| **Animation/Transition** | Sweep: cubic ease `sweepEase` (cubic bezier piecewise: 4t^3 for t<0.5, 1-(-2t+2)^3/2 for t>=0.5). Width transition: `{ duration: 0.4, ease: [0.4, 0, 0.2, 1] }`. Text swap: opacity 0.26s, blur/shift 0.34s, ease `[0.22, 1, 0.36, 1]` |
| **Constants** | `BAND_HALF = 17`, `SWEEP_START = -17`, `SWEEP_END = 117`, `TEXT_SWAP_EASE = [0.22, 1, 0.36, 1]` |
| **Background gradient** | `backgroundImage` built via `buildGradient()` — horizontal linear-gradient with color band + `textColor` outside band |
| **Blur/shift on swap** | Blurs text to 8px, shifts down 5.5px, reduces opacity to 0.58, then animates back |

### 5.2 `typewriter-effect.tsx` (121 lines) — `TypewriterEffect` / `TypewriterEffectSmooth`

#### `TypewriterEffect` (staggered character reveal)

| Aspect | Details |
|---|---|
| **Animation** | `useAnimate()`, `stagger(0.1)`, each `<span>` animates from `hidden` + `opacity:0` → `inline-block` + `opacity:1` + `width: fit-content` |
| **Trigger** | `useInView(scope)` |
| **CSS classes** | Outer: `text-base sm:text-xl md:text-3xl lg:text-5xl font-bold text-center` + user `className` |
| **Character spans** | `dark:text-white text-black opacity-0 hidden` + word-level `className` |
| **Cursor** | Blinking cursor: `inline-block rounded-sm w-[4px] h-4 md:h-6 lg:h-10 bg-blue-500` |
| **Cursor animation** | Opacity blink: `{ duration: 0.8, repeat: Infinity, repeatType: "reverse" }` |
| **Timing** | Each char delays by `stagger(0.1)`, each takes `duration: 0.3`, ease `easeInOut` |

#### `TypewriterEffectSmooth` (reveal via width expansion)

| Aspect | Details |
|---|---|
| **Animation** | `motion.div` inner width from `"0%"` → `"fit-content"`, triggered by `whileInView` |
| **CSS classes** | Outer: `flex space-x-1 my-6` + user `className`. Inner: `overflow-hidden pb-2`. Text: `text-xs sm:text-base md:text-xl lg:text:3xl xl:text-5xl font-bold` |
| **Transition** | `{ duration: 2, ease: "linear", delay: 1 }` |
| **Cursor** | Same blink as TypewriterEffect but sizes: `h-4 sm:h-6 xl:h-12` |
| **Character spans** | `dark:text-white text-black` + word-level `className` |

<?php
add_action('after_setup_theme', function () {
    add_theme_support('editor-styles');
    add_theme_support('wp-block-styles');
    add_theme_support('block-template-parts');
});

add_action('wp_head', function () {
    $uri = get_template_directory_uri();
    echo '<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="' . esc_url($uri . '/assets/favicon.svg') . '">' . "\n";
    echo '<link rel="mask-icon" href="' . esc_url($uri . '/assets/favicon.svg') . '" color="#111111">' . "\n";
});

add_action('wp_enqueue_scripts', function () {
    $theme = wp_get_theme();

    // Check if the current page uses the React Showcase template
    $use_react = false;
    if (is_singular()) {
        $template = get_page_template_slug(get_queried_object_id());
        if ($template === 'page-react-showcase.php') {
            $use_react = true;
        }
    }

    if ($use_react) {
        // Dequeue conflicting WP styles
        wp_dequeue_style('wp-block-library');
        wp_dequeue_style('wp-block-library-theme');
        wp_dequeue_style('global-styles');
        wp_dequeue_style('classic-theme-styles');

        wp_enqueue_style(
            'dist-app',
            get_template_directory_uri() . '/assets/dist-app.css',
            [],
            '1.0.0'
        );
        wp_enqueue_script(
            'dist-app',
            get_template_directory_uri() . '/assets/dist-app.js',
            [],
            '1.0.0',
            true
        );
    } else {
        wp_enqueue_style(
            'twentyfirst-showcase-styles',
            get_template_directory_uri() . '/assets/theme.css',
            [],
            $theme->get('Version')
        );

        wp_add_inline_script('wp21-frontend', '
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
    var toggle = document.getElementById("dark-mode-toggle");
    if (!toggle) return;
    if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        document.body.classList.add("dark");
    }
    toggle.addEventListener("click", function() {
        document.body.classList.toggle("dark");
    });
});
    ', 'before');
    }
}, 20);

add_action('enqueue_block_editor_assets', function () {
    $theme = wp_get_theme();
    wp_enqueue_style(
        'twentyfirst-showcase-editor-styles',
        get_template_directory_uri() . '/assets/editor.css',
        [],
        $theme->get('Version')
    );
});

add_filter('should_load_separate_core_block_assets', '__return_true');

function wp21_create_pages() {
    header('Content-Type: application/json');

    $pages = [
        [
            'title'   => 'Hybrid Showcase',
            'slug'    => 'hybrid-showcase',
            'template'=> 'page-hybrid-showcase.php',
        ],
    ];

    $results = [];
    foreach ($pages as $p) {
        $existing = get_page_by_path($p['slug'], OBJECT, 'page');
        if ($existing) {
            $results[] = ['slug' => $p['slug'], 'id' => $existing->ID, 'status' => 'exists'];
            continue;
        }
        $id = wp_insert_post([
            'post_title'   => $p['title'],
            'post_name'    => $p['slug'],
            'post_type'    => 'page',
            'post_status'  => 'publish',
            'page_template'=> $p['template'],
        ]);
        if (is_wp_error($id)) {
            $results[] = ['slug' => $p['slug'], 'error' => $id->get_error_message()];
        } else {
            $results[] = ['slug' => $p['slug'], 'id' => $id, 'status' => 'created'];
        }
    }

    echo json_encode($results);
    exit;
}

The hybrid page has the `#root` div and `WP_CONTENT` is set. The hybrid React app should mount properly. Now let me verify it works by setting some test content via the API.

Let me save a test content and verify. But actually, let me think about whether there's a problem with the WP_CONTENT initialization order. The inline script runs `before` the main hybrid JS, so `WP_CONTENT` should be set before the React app mounts. But there might be a timing issue...

Actually, looking at the `wp_add_inline_script` call with `'before'` position: this adds the script right before the `wp21-hybrid` script tag in the HTML. So the execution order is:
1. `<script id="wp21-hybrid-data" type="application/json">{}</script>`
2. `<script id="wp21-hybrid-js-before">var el = document.getElementById("wp21-hybrid-data"); if (el) { try { window.WP_CONTENT = JSON.parse(el.textContent); } catch(e) {} }</script>`
3. `<script id="wp21-hybrid-js" src="...hybrid-main-CdIVSn9-.js"></script>`

The issue: the `wp21-hybrid-data` script has `type="application/json"`, which means the browser won't execute it as JavaScript. It's just data. The `js-before` script reads from it. This should work fine because the JSON script element is in the DOM before the js-before runs.

But there's a subtlety: `getElementById("wp21-hybrid-data")` should find the element since it's rendered before the js-before script. Yes, this should work.

Now, the hybrid React app will see `window.WP_CONTENT = {}` (empty object). When it does `window.WP_CONTENT?.hero?.badge ?? "21st.dev Showcase"`, it will get `undefined ?? "21st.dev Showcase"`, which gives "21st.dev Showcase". 

But wait - what if the user saves content that only partially overrides? For example, if they only set `hero.badge`, the `hero.diaWords` would still use defaults. That should work with `??`.

Actually, there might be a problem. If the user saves:
```json
{"hero": {"badge": "My Custom Badge"}}
```

Then `window.WP_CONTENT` will be `{hero: {badge: "My Custom Badge"}}`. Then:
- `window.WP_CONTENT?.hero?.badge ?? "21st.dev Showcase"` → "My Custom Badge" (correct)
- `window.WP_CONTENT?.hero?.diaWords ?? defaultDiaWords` → `undefined ?? ["smooth.", ...]` → ["smooth.", ...] (correct)

This works because `??` only replaces `null`/`undefined`, and nested undefined properties cascade properly.

Here's what was built:

## Hybrid Approach Complete

### Three pages now at your disposal:

| Page | URL | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Showcase | `/` or `/showcase/` | Gutenberg-block version (editable in Site Editor) |
| React Original | `/react-showcase/` | Pixel-perfect static dist (not editable, reference) |
| **Hybrid Showcase** | **`/hybrid-showcase/`** | **React app + WordPress data (editable, pixel-perfect)** |

### How the hybrid works:

1. **React rendering engine** — The exact same Vite-built React app from `src/App-hybrid.tsx` (same components, same CSS, same animations). All text content reads from `window.WP_CONTENT` with hardcoded defaults as fallback.

2. **WordPress data layer** — Content is stored as a JSON option (`wp21_showcase_content`) in the WordPress database. The PHP template passes it to the browser via `wp_localize_script`.

3. **Admin editing** — Go to **Settings → Showcase Content** in the WordPress admin. Paste in your content as JSON with the same structure as the defaults. Any fields you omit fall back to the pixel-perfect hardcoded defaults.

### To edit content:
```
WP Admin → Settings → Showcase Content → paste JSON → Save
```

The JSON structure mirrors the section hierarchy. You only need to include the fields you want to override — everything else uses the defaults that match the React original exactly.
how can you turn it into a visual editor analyze the most effective with highest accuracy or UI

The user wants me to analyze the best approach for turning the current hybrid showcase (which uses a JSON textarea in the WordPress admin) into a visual editor. They want to know the most effective approach with highest accuracy or UI quality.

Let me think about the options:

1. **WordPress Customizer** - Uses the built-in WordPress Customizer API with live preview. High accuracy since changes are reflected in real-time in the iframe preview. The Customizer API is mature but limited in terms of complex UI.

2. **Advanced Custom Fields (ACF)** - Provides a visual field editor with WYSIWYG, color pickers, repeaters, etc. Very mature, widely used. Could create a clean UI for each section.

3. **Gutenberg Block Editor for the hybrid page** - Use `wp.blocks` and `wp.data` to create a custom post type or page that uses blocks to build the content, then render it via React.

4. **React-based admin page** - Build a React SPA for the admin that mirrors the front-end layout with inline editing. Highest accuracy since the editor can literally be the same components. But most development effort.

5. **WordPress Block Editor (FSE) with custom blocks** - Create custom blocks for each section that mirror the React components. This is what the original Gutenberg version does, but it doesn't match pixel-perfect.

6. **Third-party page builders (Elementor, Beaver Builder, etc.)** - Use an existing page builder. High UI quality but would require adapting the React components to work within the builder.

Let me think about what "highest accuracy" means - it means the visual editor should produce output that matches the React original as closely as possible. And "highest UI" means the editing experience should be intuitive and pleasant.

Let me analyze each option:

### Option 1: Advanced Custom Fields (ACF) - Blocks or Options Page
**Pros:**
- Mature, well-documented, extensive field types (repeater, WYSIWYG, color picker, text, etc.)
- Can create an options page with all fields
- Can create ACF blocks that render directly in the Gutenberg editor
- Preview available in the editor
- Relatively fast to implement
- Non-technical users can use it

**Cons:**
- Requires ACF Pro for some features (repeater, flexible content)
- The preview won't have the React animations (static preview only)
- Editing experience isn't pixel-perfect - it's form-based
- ACF blocks render in Gutenberg which won't match React exactly

**Accuracy: Medium** (form-based editing, no live preview of the actual React components)
**UI Quality: High** (well-designed field UI, intuitive)

### Option 2: React Admin Page (SPA) with live preview
**Pros:**
- Can reuse the exact same React components for the preview
- WYSIWYG - what you see is what you get, pixel-perfect
- Highest accuracy possible
- Can be built as a WordPress admin page (within wp-admin)

**Cons:**
- Most development effort
- Need to rebuild the form UI
- Need to manage loading of the React app within wp-admin
- WordPress admin styling conflicts

**Accuracy: Very High** (live preview with actual components)
**UI Quality: High** (custom React UI, inline editing)

### Option 3: Block Editor (Gutenberg) Custom Post Type
**Pros:**
- Uses the familiar WordPress block editor
- Can create custom blocks with the React components
- Rich text editing built-in
- Can add custom InspectorControls for colors, etc.

**Cons:**
- Gutenberg blocks still won't match the pixel-perfect React rendering
- Very complex to implement custom dynamic blocks
- Limited animation support in editor
- The rendered output would differ from the React version

**Accuracy: Low-Medium** (Gutenberg output ≠ React output)
**UI Quality: High** (familiar block editor)

### Option 4: WordPress Customizer
**Pros:**
- Built-in live preview (iframe-based)
- Can show the actual front-end with React rendered
- Sections/panels for organization
- No additional plugin needed

**Cons:**
- Limited field types (text, textarea, color, etc.)
- No repeater fields without custom JS
- The preview loads the entire page in an iframe (might have issues with React re-rendering)
- The customizer API is showing its age
- Complex for deeply nested data (like arrays of variants)

**Accuracy: High** (iframe preview of actual page)
**UI Quality: Medium** (dated UI, limited controls)

### Option 5: ACF + React Preview Hybrid
**Pros:**
- ACF handles the admin UI (fields, saving, validation)
- A separate React preview page shows the actual front-end
- Best of both worlds
- Much less dev effort than building a full React SPA

**Cons:**
- Still two separate experiences (edit in ACF, preview separately)
- ACF fields can't provide live React preview

**Accuracy: Medium-High** (actual React output on preview)
**UI Quality: High** (ACF field UI is polished)

### My Recommendation: ACF Options Page with Repeater Fields

Actually, the best approach considering effort vs. accuracy vs. UI quality would be:

**Option 6: WordPress Admin Page with React-based visual editor + iframe preview**

This would:
1. Create a custom admin page that loads the React admin editor
2. The editor shows a simplified live preview of the showcase
3. Each section has inline-editable text areas
4. Save updates the `wp21_showcase_content` option
5. The front-end `page-hybrid-showcase.php` reads the same option

This is essentially what the user already has (JSON textarea) but with a visual editing interface.

Or even better:

**Option 7: Custom admin page with per-section form fields + side-by-side preview**

This would be:
- A WordPress admin page with sections
- Each section has text inputs, color pickers, etc.
- A live preview iframe or React component shows changes in real-time
- The data is stored as the same JSON option
- No ACF dependency

Let me think about which is truly the best in terms of:
1. **Accuracy** - How closely the editor output matches the final rendered page
2. **UI Quality** - How good the editing experience is
3. **Development effort** - How much code needs to be written
4. **Maintainability** - How easy it is to change later

The best option is to build a **custom WordPress admin page with a React-based visual editor**. Here's why:

- **Accuracy**: The editor can use the exact same React components for the preview. When you edit text, you see it in the actual component. This is pixel-perfect accurate.
- **UI Quality**: Can build a polished, modern UI with inline editing, drag-and-drop reordering of variants, color pickers with swatches, etc.
- **Effort**: Medium-high. Need to build a React app specifically for the admin, but the components already exist.
- **Maintainability**: High. The data structure stays the same (JSON option), the front-end doesn't change at all.

Let me think about a simpler approach that still gives great results...

Actually, the **simplest** approach that gives high accuracy and good UI would be:

**Option 8: Use the WordPress Customizer with a custom panel and iframe preview**

The Customizer already has iframe-based live preview. We just need to:
1. Register a customizer panel
2. Add sections for each showcase section
3. Add controls for each text field
4. The preview URL points to the hybrid showcase page
5. Use JavaScript in the preview to read the customizer values and update the React app

This would give us:
- Live preview of the actual front-end (including animations)
- WordPress-native UI
- All the customizer's built-in features (save drafts, schedule, etc.)
- No additional plugin dependency

But the Customizer has limitations:
- No repeater fields (can't add/remove variants dynamically)
- No color picker arrays
- The iframe preview might struggle with React hydration/re-rendering

Actually, the best approach considering everything is probably a **custom admin page with per-field inputs and a live preview**. Let me outline the plan more concretely:

## Recommended Plan: React Admin Visual Editor

### Architecture
1. **Admin page** (`/wp-admin/admin.php?page=wp21-visual-editor`)
2. **React app** loaded in the admin that:
   - Shows a split-screen: form on the left, preview on the right
   - Each section has collapsible fields
   - Text inputs, color pickers, array editors for words
   - The preview is the actual hybrid React components rendered with the current values
   - "Save" button saves the JSON to the `wp21_showcase_content` option
   - "Reset to defaults" button restores defaults

3. **Data flow**:
   - Admin React app reads initial data from `wp_localize_script`
   - User edits fields → React state updates → preview re-renders
   - Save → POST to REST API → updates `wp21_showcase_content`
   - Front-end page reads same option → renders with new content

### Key advantage
The preview uses the EXACT same React components (`DiaText`, `TypewriterEffectSmooth`, etc.) that the front-end uses. So the preview IS the actual rendered output. This gives 100% accuracy.

### Implementation steps:
1. Create `src/admin/AdminApp.tsx` — the admin editor React app
2. Create form components for each section
3. Include preview components that import from `../components/ui/`
4. Build with Vite to theme assets
5. Create PHP admin page that enqueues the editor
6. Add REST API endpoint for saving content

## Analysis: Visual Editor Approaches

Ranked by accuracy + UI quality + effort:

### Option A: Custom Admin Page with React Live Preview ⭐ **Best**
Build a React admin app with split-screen: form on left, live preview on right. The preview uses your **exact same React components** (DiaText, Typewriter, etc.), so it's pixel-perfect. Edits reflect instantly. Saves to the same JSON option.

- **Accuracy**: 100% (same components render the preview)
- **UI Quality**: Excellent (modern, inline color pickers, collapsible sections, drag-and-drop variant ordering)
- **Effort**: Medium-high (need to build admin React app + form UI)

### Option B: WordPress Customizer with iframe Preview
Uses the built-in Customizer API. The iframe loads the actual hybrid showcase page. Changes push via `postMessage` and update the React app dynamically.

- **Accuracy**: High (preview is the real page with animations)
- **UI Quality**: Medium (Customizer is dated, no repeaters for variant arrays)
- **Effort**: Medium (native API, but complex for nested arrays)

### Option C: ACF Options Page with Field Groups
Uses Advanced Custom Fields Pro. Each text field gets a proper input (WYSIWYG, color picker, repeater). No live preview of React output.

- **Accuracy**: Low-Medium (form-based, no React preview)
- **UI Quality**: High (polished ACF UI, non-technical users)
- **Effort**: Low (just configure fields) but requires ACF Pro

### Option D: Keep JSON textarea + Preview button
The current approach with a "Preview" button that opens the hybrid page in a new tab.

- **Accuracy**: N/A (no visual editing)
- **UI Quality**: Low (raw JSON editing)
- **Effort**: None (already done)

---

**I recommend Option A** — a custom React admin page with live preview. It's the only approach that gives pixel-perfect accuracy because the preview **is** the actual React app. The implementation would reuse most of your existing components, just wrapping them in an admin layout with form controls.

the hybrid approach we did earlier, will it work and how so for a multi-page website with sub pages like /homepage, /cars etc

The user is asking about how the hybrid approach (React app + WordPress data layer) would work for a multi-page website with sub-pages like `/homepage`, `/cars`, etc. They want to understand the architecture and if it scales.

Let me think through this carefully and provide a thorough analysis. I'm in plan/read-only mode, so I should only analyze and plan, not make any changes.

Key considerations for multi-page:
1. Each page needs its own content data
2. Navigation/routing between pages
3. Shared components vs page-specific components
4. How to manage content in WordPress for each page
5. Build size/performance implications

Let me think about the architecture options:

**Option 1: Single-page React app with client-side routing**
- One React app, one build
- Uses React Router for `/homepage`, `/cars`, etc.
- `WP_CONTENT` provides content for ALL pages (or fetches per-page via REST API)
- Pros: Single build, fast navigation, shared state
- Cons: Larger initial bundle, SEO concerns (need SSR/SSG)

**Option 2: Multi-page React app (separate builds per page)**
- Each page is a separate Vite build entry point
- `/homepage` → `homepage-main.js`, `/cars` → `cars-main.js`
- Each page has its own `WP_CONTENT` or fetches page-specific content
- Pros: Smaller bundles, page-specific optimization
- Cons: Multiple builds, full page reloads, duplicate shared code

**Option 3: Hybrid - Single React app with separate data per page**
- Same React app build loaded on every page
- WordPress determines which page content to inject
- React app switches sections/content based on page identifier
- Pros: Single build, no routing library needed, each page is a standalone WordPress page
- Cons: Need to manage multiple WordPress pages with the same template

Actually, the simplest and most practical approach for a WordPress-integrated multi-page:

**Option 4: WordPress page templates with shared React app**
- Each page (homepage, cars, etc.) uses the same PHP template (`page-hybrid-showcase.php`)
- WordPress page meta stores per-page content as JSON post meta (not a site-wide option)
- The React app reads `WP_CONTENT` which includes a `pageId` or sections specific to that page
- Different templates can load different React entry points or use the same one with different data

This is the most natural WordPress pattern. Let me elaborate on this.

Actually, let me think about what makes the most sense for the user's stated use case: a multi-page website with `/homepage`, `/cars`, etc. This sounds like they want to use the hybrid React approach for multiple distinct pages, not just one showcase.

The key question is: does each page have a completely different set of React components, or do they share the same components but with different content?

If each page is completely different (different React components), then:
- Each page needs its own React build
- Each page can have its own content in WordPress

If pages share the same components with different content (like a template pattern):
- One React build, one template, per-page content via WordPress meta fields

Let me present the options clearly to the user and ask clarifying questions.

Great question. The hybrid approach absolutely works for multi-page — here's how the architecture scales:

## Core Architecture for Multi-Page

```
Page Request (/homepage, /cars, etc.)
         │
         ▼
  WordPress routes to the Hybrid template
         │
         ├── WP determines which page this is (post ID / slug)
         ├── Fetches per-page content from post meta (not a global option)
         └── Passes page-specific JSON to the React app
                │
                ▼
         Same React build, different data
```

## Two Patterns

### A) Same template, same React build, different per-page content
Each page uses `page-hybrid-showcase.php` but stores its content in **post meta** (not a global option). The React app renders different sections based on the page ID/content structure. Best for pages with similar layout patterns.

**Content example for `/cars`:**
```json
{"hero":{"heading":"Find your dream car","diaWords":["fast.","luxurious.","electric."]},
 "features":{"cards":[...tesla data...]},
 "contact":{"heading":"Book a test drive"}}
```

### B) Separate template per page type, separate React builds
`page-cars.php` loads `cars-main.js` (a Vite build with car-specific components). `page-homepage.php` loads `homepage-main.js`. Each has its own component tree and content structure. Best when pages are fundamentally different.

## Key architectural decisions

**1. Content storage:** Per-page post meta (not a global option) — this is the WordPress way. Each page's JSON content is stored as `_hybrid_content` meta, retrieved automatically based on the current page.

**2. Shared React app pattern:** One Vite build loaded everywhere. The app checks `window.PAGE_ID` and `window.PAGE_CONTENT` (or a single `WP_CONTENT` with a `pageId` field) and renders the appropriate sections. Shared components (header, footer, navigation) render identically across all pages.

**3. Content editing:** Settings page → select which page → visual editor saves to that page's meta.

**4. Page routing:** Let WordPress handle routing (it already knows which page is being viewed). No React Router needed — the PHP template passes the page identity to the React app.

---

**Question for you:** Will all pages share the **same component set** (DiaText, Typewriter, ContactForm, etc.) just with different text/colors/images? Or does `/cars` need completely **different React components** (e.g., a car configurator, image gallery, booking widget)?

This determines whether you need one React build (simpler) or multiple builds (more flexible).

Let me think about the best architecture for this...

The key building blocks:

2. **Hybrid template**: Loads the single React app + passes all page contents
3. **React app**: Uses React Router to determine which page to show, reads content from `WP_CONTENT[route]`

For the visual editor part (the user's original question), since they have different pages with different components, the editor needs to be:
- Page-aware (show different fields per page)
- Component-aware (different pages have different editable sections)

This is getting complex. Let me present a clear plan.

Right — so it's a full multi-page React SPA with client-side routing. The WordPress hybrid layer needs to adapt. Here's the plan:

## Architecture

### One React app, one catch-all template

```
react-router routes:  /homepage  /cars  /about  ...
                            \      |      /
                             \     |     /
                        Single hybrid template
                          (handles ALL URLs)
                                │
                    ┌───────────┴───────────┐
                    │                       │
            WP_CONTENT = {           React app reads
              homepage: {...},       current route via
              cars: {...},           react-router,
              about: {...},          renders matching page
              settings: {...}        with its content
            }
```

### Implementation steps

**1. Catch-all WordPress page template**
- Create `page-hybrid-spa.php` template
- Add a rewrite rule that sends ALL unrouted URLs to this template (or use a specific parent page slug)
- The template loads the single React build for every sub-path

**2. Content storage**
- A single WordPress option or a custom post type (`hybrid_pages`) mapping `route → content JSON`
- The template loads ALL route contents upfront and passes as `WP_CONTENT`

**3. Admin visual editor (the part you asked about)**
The editor needs to be page-aware and component-aware. Best approach:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Page: [homepage ▼]   Component tree         │
│  ┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────┐  │
│  │ Form panel          │ Live preview      │  │
│  │                     │ (iframe loading   │  │
│  │ Hero:               │  the actual       │  │
│  │  Heading [_________]│  React app with   │  │
│  │  DiaWords [...     ]│  current edits)   │  │
│  │  Colors  [■ ■ ■ ■ ]│                    │  │
│  │                     │  postMessage →     │  │
│  │ Features:           │  WP_CONTENT       │  │
│  │  Title  [_________] │  updates in real- │  │
│  │  Cards: [+ Add]     │  time             │  │
│  │   [Title___][Desc__]│                    │  │
│  └─────────────────────┴──────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The **live preview** loads the actual hybrid page in an iframe with `?preview=1`. The admin panel sends `postMessage({ type: "updateContent", data: {...} })`. The React app listens and re-renders with the edited data.

**4. Per-page component awareness**
Since different routes have different component trees, the editor needs to know what to show. Two approaches:

| Approach | How it works | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Declare schema per route** | Each route exports an `editorSchema` that defines which fields are editable and their form types | Accurate per-page, type-safe | Requires manual schema per route |
| **Introspect from React tree** | A dev script walks the component tree and generates a form schema | Zero manual work | Fragile, harder to customize |

I'd recommend **declaring a schema per route** since you already know which components each page uses:

```tsx
// In the React app, each page exports:
export const editorSchema = {
  hero: {
    badge: { type: "text", label: "Badge" },
    diaWords: { type: "array-of-strings", label: "Cycling Words" },
    description: { type: "textarea", label: "Description" },
  },
  features: {
    cards: { type: "repeater", label: "Feature Cards", fields: {
      title: { type: "text" },
      desc: { type: "textarea" }
    }}
  }
}
```

### Build order

1. Add catch-all rewrite rule + hybrid template
2. Add multi-page content storage (per-route JSON in post meta or custom table)
3. Build the admin visual editor (form panel + iframe preview with `postMessage` bridge)
4. Wire the React app to accept `WP_CONTENT` updates via `postMessage` in preview mode
5. Connect admin save → WordPress REST API → stored per-route

Want me to draft the rewrite rule + catch-all template, or go deeper into the visual editor UI?

Now I have a complete picture. Let me also check what Elementor hooks/file structure looks like so I can make an accurate plan.

Here's my analysis:

**Current state:**
- `wp21-animations` plugin has Gutenberg blocks that work via:
  - PHP render callbacks that output specific HTML with data attributes
  - `frontend.js` (vanilla JS) that reads those data attributes and performs animations
  - `theme.css` with CSS for gradient button (with `@property`), text glitch (with `@keyframes`), dia text, text cycle, typewriter cursor

**Key insight:** The `frontend.js` already does all animation work in vanilla JS with `requestAnimationFrame`, `IntersectionObserver`, and `setInterval` — no React dependency needed on the frontend! This means it works perfectly with **any** HTML output that has the right CSS classes and data attributes.

**Elementor approach:**
Instead of Gutenberg blocks, create **Elementor widgets** that:
1. Output the exact same HTML structure as the current Gutenberg render callbacks
2. Use Elementor's control API for the admin UI (text fields, color pickers, repeaters)
3. Reuse the existing `frontend.js` for all animations
4. Reuse the existing `theme.css` for all styles

This leverages ALL existing code — only the widget registration changes from Gutenberg to Elementor.

Let me now plan the full file structure and implementation.

The plugin already has:
- `wp21-animations.php` - main plugin file
- `src/blocks/*/block.json` - Gutenberg block definitions
- `assets/frontend.js` - animation engine
- `assets/theme.css` → needs to be moved/loaded by the plugin

Wait, theme.css is in the theme, not the plugin. For Elementor widgets, the CSS needs to be available. I should either:
1. Move the CSS to the plugin
2. Or enqueue theme.css from the plugin

Actually, the theme.css is already loaded by the theme for non-React pages. For Elementor pages, we need to ensure the CSS is loaded. The cleanest approach: move the relevant CSS into the plugin and have the plugin enqueue it.

Let me draft a comprehensive plan:

## Plan: Elementor Animation Widgets

### Files to create/modify:

1. **`wp21-elementor-widgets.php`** - New plugin (or extend existing)
   - Register with Elementor
   - Define 6 widget classes
   - Enqueue `frontend.js` and `widgets.css`

2. **`assets/widgets.css`** - Combined CSS for all widgets
   - Copy relevant styles from `theme.css` + `index.css`
   - Gradient button `@property` + styles
   - Text glitch `@keyframes` + styles
   - Dia text background-clip
   - Typewriter cursor blink
   - Text reveal transitions
   - Text cycle transitions

3. **Widget classes** (each in its own file or inline in the plugin):

   a. **`DiaText_Widget`**
      - Controls: Text (repeater), Colors (repeater), Duration, Repeat toggle, Repeat Delay
      - Render: Same HTML as `wp21_render_dia_text()`

   b. **`Typewriter_Widget`**
      - Controls: Words (repeater with text + class), Cursor Color
      - Render: Same HTML as `wp21_render_typewriter()`

   c. **`GradientButton_Widget`**
      - Controls: Button Text, Link (URL), Variant select (default/variant)
      - Render: Same HTML as `wp21_render_gradient_button()`

   d. **`TextGlitch_Widget`**
      - Controls: Text, Hover Text
      - Render: Same HTML as `wp21_render_text_glitch()`

   e. **`TextReveal_Widget`**
      - Controls: Content (textarea/WYSIWYG), Direction
      - Render: Same HTML as `wp21_render_text_reveal()`

   f. **`TextCycle_Widget`**
      - Controls: Words (repeater), Interval
      - Render: Same HTML as `wp21_render_text_cycle()`

### Page building in Elementor:

1. Create page structure matching the React app:
   - Full-width sections with matching background colors
   - Same padding (py-24 = 96px, px-4 = 16px)
   - Same border treatments (border-y, border-t)
   - Same typography hierarchy

2. Insert custom widgets in the right order:
   - Hero: DiaText, headings
   - Features: Standard Elementor heading + icon/list widgets for cards
   - DiaText variants: 3 DiaText widgets
   - Typewriter: 2 Typewriter widgets
   - Gradient Button: 2 Gradient Button widgets
   - Text Reveal: 1 Text Reveal widget
   - Text Glitch: 1 Text Glitch widget
   - Text Cycle: 1 Text Cycle widget
   - Combined Demo: DiaText + Typewriter
   - Code Export: Standard HTML/code widget
   - Contact: Standard form (or custom SmoothInput widget)

### Accuracy assessment:

| Component | Elementor | Custom Widget | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hero section layout | ✅ Native (section, column) | — | High |
| Hero DiaText | — | ✅ DiaText | **100%** (same JS) |
| Feature cards | ✅ Heading + text + border | — | High (manual spacing) |
| DiaText variants | — | ✅ DiaText | **100%** |
| Typewriter | — | ✅ Typewriter | **100%** |
| Gradient Button | — | ✅ GradientButton | **100%** |
| Text Reveal | 🟡 Scroll effects | Could use either | Medium-High |
| Text Glitch | — | ✅ TextGlitch | **100%** |
| Text Cycle | — | ✅ TextCycle | **100%** |
| Combined Demo | — | DiaText + Typewriter | **100%** |
| Code block | ✅ HTML widget | — | Medium (monospace) |
| Contact form | ✅ Form widget | — | Medium (no animated caret) |
| Animations | ✅ Entrance anims | — | Medium (different feel) |
| Dark mode | — | — | Needs CSS class toggle |

### Gaps vs React:

1. **Dark mode toggle** — Elementor doesn't support `.dark` class toggling natively. Need a small JS snippet.

2. **SmoothInput** — Elementor's form widget has standard inputs. Animated caret requires custom widget.

3. **TextReveal scroll animation** — Elementor Pro has scroll effects, but the per-word fade-in is custom. The TextReveal widget handles this.

4. **Responsive font sizes** — The React app uses `text-4xl sm:text-5xl md:text-6xl lg:text-7xl`. Elementor supports responsive sizing but needs manual setup per breakpoint.

5. **Hero radial gradient** — Elementor supports background gradients natively.

6. **Code export "reusable exports" tags** — Can use Elementor's inline positioning or a list widget.

7. **Spacing** — All spacing values (py-24=96px, gap-20=80px, etc.) need to be manually set in Elementor section/column settings.

This plan is solid and achievable. Let me present it clearly.

Now I have a complete picture. Here's the plan.

## Analysis

**Good news:** `frontend.js` is already vanilla JS (no React) — it animates via `data-*` attributes on HTML elements. Every Gutenberg block is just HTML + the existing JS/CSS. Elementor widgets can output the **exact same HTML** and get the **exact same animation behavior**.

**Bad news:** Elementor has no built-in dark mode toggle, and its animations are CSS-only (no gradient sweep, typewriter, glitch keyframes, word cycling).

## Plan: Elementor Animation Widgets Plugin

### New plugin: `wp21-elementor-widgets/`

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `wp21-elementor-widgets.php` | Plugin bootstrap, Elementor hooks, widget registration |
| `assets/widgets.css` | All animation CSS (extracted from theme.css + index.css for @property, @keyframes) |
| `widgets/class-dia-text-widget.php` | DiaText widget |
| `widgets/class-typewriter-widget.php` | Typewriter widget |
| `widgets/class-gradient-button-widget.php` | Gradient Button widget |
| `widgets/class-text-glitch-widget.php` | Text Glitch widget |
| `widgets/class-text-reveal-widget.php` | Text Reveal widget |
| `widgets/class-text-cycle-widget.php` | Text Cycle widget |

### Each widget:
- Registers Elementor controls matching the animation params (repeater for words, color picker for colors, number for duration, toggle for repeat)
- `render()` outputs **identical HTML** to the current Gutenberg render callbacks
- Reuses existing `frontend.js` (enqueued by the plugin)
- Reuses existing CSS (enqueued from `assets/widgets.css`)

### Building the page in Elementor:

| Section | Content + Elementor tools |
|---|---|
| Hero | Section (100vh, radial gradient bg) → custom DiaText widget + Elementor heading widgets for "21st.dev Showcase" label and description → animated down arrow (CSS) |
| Feature cards | Elementor `section > 3 columns` with border, heading, text widgets |
| DiaText variants | custom DiaText widgets (3 instances with different color/word configs) |
| Typewriter | custom Typewriter widgets (2 instances) |
| Gradient Button | custom GradientButton widgets (2 instances) |
| Text Reveal | custom TextReveal widget |
| Text Glitch | custom TextGlitch widget |
| Text Cycle | custom TextCycle widget |
| Combined Demo | custom DiaText + Typewriter |
| Code block | Elementor HTML widget (code block) + native heading/text |
| Contact | Elementor Form widget (native — animated caret would need a custom SmoothInput widget but is low priority) |
| Footer | Elementor HTML widget |

### Accuracy per component:

| Widget | Expected accuracy |
|---|---|
| DiaText | **100%** — exact same HTML data attributes → exact same JS animation |
| Typewriter | **100%** — same |
| GradientButton | **100%** — same HTML/CSS |
| TextGlitch | **100%** — same HTML/CSS |
| TextReveal | **100%** — same HTML/data attributes → same IntersectionObserver JS |
| TextCycle | **100%** — same HTML/data attributes → same JS |
| Layout/spacing | ~95% — requires manual matching of 96px padding, 80px gaps, 16px column padding, etc. |
| Dark mode | ~80% — needs `.dark` class on `<body>` + small JS snippet for toggle |
| Contact form | ~70% — no animated caret, but functions correctly |

### Dark mode plan:
- `.dark` class toggle JS (existing code in functions.php can be reused)
- Widgets CSS uses `.dark` overrides (already in theme.css, will copy to widgets.css)
- Toggle button added via Elementor HTML widget

### What you'll edit in Elementor:
Every text string, color, animation duration, and word list is editable through Elementor's panel UI — no JSON, no code. The animation JS/CSS is untouched (pixel-perfect from the React source).

---

Want me to proceed with building this? I'll start with the plugin structure and the DiaText widget as the first deliverable so you can verify the pattern before I build all 6.
